t: The best thing I did at Goldman Sachs was talk my way onto someone else's janky side project. Mehti prayed next to me every day. One afternoon on the way out I asked how it was going. I meant it as a greeting. He heard it as a question about his startup, and started telling me everything. He'd coded it himself and it barely worked. The idea was that every like turns into a penny for charity, so content creators could fundraise just by posting. I couldn't stop thinking about it. So I asked if I could work on it. I was 19. The whole company was two co-founders, one engineer, and me. We got into an accelerator called Fast Forward in Stratford. My Goldman apprenticeship was three days work, two days uni, so I started skipping the uni days and going to the programme instead. I didn't have a growth strategy. I just started posting about what we were building on Twitter because it felt like the obvious thing to do. Then I found a hook that made people finally get what MiniDeed was, and one tweet went viral. That turned into a funnel into a Telegram community, and it kept growing on its own. Then Ramadan hit. High profile Muslim creators started reaching out, New Arab, Islam Channel. We ran a campaign and the numbers got kind of mad. 26,000 donations, 800,000 taps, 47,000 posts across 26 countries. oh btw - he never did tell me how he was doing.

You ever see a cause on social media and feel helpless because the only thing you can do is just raise awareness? That’s why we created MiniDeed, an app where you raise money for the causes you care about by creating posts and donate pennies to other causes!
never I thought I’d read minideed praise in another language in just 2 month but we’re already here. MiniDeed is going international! 🇮🇹 ✈️
Having a lot of fun presenting @MiniDeed at @FFWDLondon. Been sharing your comments and ideas, they love it! Keep it up!

MiniDeed is really precious tonight with all the wonderful MiniDeeders sharing their mental health struggles with the #MiniStruggle hashtag. I love the safe space it’s creating for people to open up in this way

This MiniDeed journey has been amazing thank you all you MiniDeeders that have joined us on this journey this year. Without you we couldn’t have reached over 25 countries and raised £26k through just likes ♥️ 2021 is about to be even better with you guys you’re not ready...

We raised £26,000 for charity through an app where every like was worth 1p. We made exactly £0 in revenue. I was 18. First year of my degree apprenticeship at Goldman Sachs. I met the co-founder in the basement prayer room. We'd just finished praying and I asked him how he was doing, just being polite, and he mistook it as me asking how the app was doing. This man was probably mid-thirties, been at Goldman for years, and he just started telling me about this social media platform where every like triggered a micro-donation to charity. I had no idea what he was talking about. But I was in. That's how MiniDeed started for me. 1p, 2p, 5p. Tiny amounts that added up across 25 countries over two years. We onboarded Islamic Relief, Human Relief Foundation, a bunch of smaller orgs. We got featured in The New Arab. And somehow built a community where people were opening up about mental health because the whole vibe was just different. Users told us it was the only app where they felt safe doing that. Honestly watching the live donation ticker go up was more addictive than any MRR dashboard I've looked at since (and I say that as someone who now stares at dashboards for a living). We never figured out how to make money from it. Donations still trickle through the app daily, years later. But it was my first real taste of building something and I think about it all the time. 18 years old, sitting in Goldman Sachs by day, shipping a charity app by night. It led me to build the highest-rated burger joint in London. And now Draper.
In love with my new desk 😍 ft my minideed mug

I didn’t plan to build Simply Smashed – we built it to survive. In early 2020, just as the lockdown was being announced, my parents boarded a flight back to Bangladesh, leaving my brother, Sifat Ahmed, and me to manage our family’s Italian restaurant in East London. What was meant to be a routine trip turned into a months-long ordeal. Suddenly, we were on our own, struggling to keep the business afloat without knowing when our parents could return. Those months were some of the most intense and challenging of my life. Between finishing my degree apprenticeship at Goldman Sachs, navigating repatriation flights to bring my parents, and even dealing with a burglary at the restaurant, it felt like we were up against a storm. We knew we had to go back to basics. We transformed the delivery experience, launched two critical campaigns, and even got featured on Islam Channel for our efforts to donate pizzas to NHS staff during the pandemic – all while operating from the red. This is why community is one of the foundations of our brand. Simply Smashed was born out of sheer necessity. It wasn’t a start from scratch; it was a start from survival. Today, we're proud to be a family-run business as the highest rated burger joint in London (4.9* 1800+ Google reviews) with a story grounded in resilience and community. Loved speaking to Areeb Siddiqui on his podcast about our journey and what's to come next!

We sold burgers from the back of a flower shop. And it saved our restaurant. Our full-service Italian restaurant was dying after COVID hit. My brother had what seemed like the worst idea ever: "Let's share space with a flower shop and focus on delivery only." I thought he'd lost his mind. Our runway was coming to an end. But when you're drowning, you grab any lifeline. He found the perfect partner - a flower shop that donated profits to Pakistani hospitals. Value-aligned. Rent-splitting. Life-saving. The setup was surreal. Customers walked through rows of roses to pick up our burgers. TikTokers filmed themselves navigating bouquets for delivery pickups. One tweet still makes me laugh: "Only in Tower Hamlets would you find Bengali brothers selling burgers from the back of a flower shop." But here's what happened behind those flowers: We stripped everything to the bone. No dining room overheads. No server wages. Just us, a £100 grill, and laser focus on the perfect burger. Whilst other restaurants fought to save their dining rooms, we mastered what people actually wanted: delivery excellence. The "backwards" move taught us forward thinking. That flower shop partnership didn't just keep us alive. It made us London's highest-rated burger joint. Pride kills more businesses than competition ever will. I see entrepreneurs clinging to status symbols whilst their bank accounts drain. The fancy office. The prestigious location. The "way things should be done." Sometimes the most successful move looks like complete failure from the outside. Sometimes you have to bloom where you're planted, even if it's behind the roses. What would your business look like if you stripped away everything except what actually drives results?

Three years ago, we borrowed a projector. This summer, we packed out a living room. When we opened Simply Smashed three years ago, it was during the Euros final. At the time, we were a dark kitchen, but we started getting requests to show the game. So, I borrowed a projector from a friend, put together some tables, and screened the final in-store. It felt like something was missing—a Muslim-friendly atmosphere to watch live sports. That night planted a seed. We weathered the storm as a dark kitchen, built our reputation, and became a Top Eats vendor on Uber Eats, a certification awarded to the platform's highest-performing restaurants. When we finally had enough together, we renovated the space with one clear goal: to create a communal living room. A Muslim-friendly "third space" where people could gather, relax, and feel at home. Fast forward to this summer, and we hosted our second Euros final. Alhamdulillah, we’ve come a long way. We’ve added two screens, brought in sofas, and designed the space ourselves to look and feel like a living room. The atmosphere was incredible, and the place was full. Our vision is to create a true third space for Muslims. If non-Muslims have pubs to see their regular community, why shouldn’t Muslims have something similar? An alcohol-free, music-free space where everyone, Muslim or not, can find their community outside the pub. It’s humbling to reflect on how far we’ve come, and it’s exciting to think about what’s next. Who knows where we’ll be by the next Euros, inshaAllah?

We went from 50-minute order times to 8 minutes. This simple screen represents everything we've been through to get here. Two years ago, I was crawling behind fridges looking for lost receipts. We were taking orders on notepads in the back of a flower shop. Scribbling down orders, crumpling paper, throwing it to the back of house. When we "upgraded" to receipts, we printed doubles because we kept losing them. Internet goes out? Back to notepad chaos. Rush hour? Receipts everywhere. Behind fridges, through floor cracks, completely vanished. Customers asking "where's my food?" while we're on our hands and knees searching. Kitchen screaming over the noise because that's the only way to communicate. If you've worked hospitality, you know this stress. If you haven't, you have no idea what happens behind those kitchen doors. The thing is, people don't see this part. They don't see the 50-minute wait times we used to have to get here. The frustrated faces. The orders we had to remake because we lost the ticket. This screen might look standard to you. To me, it represents every chaotic shift we survived to get here. Clean. Digital. Orders flow seamlessly from front to back. I had a moment today just staring at this screen. Feeling proud of how far we've come. From the back of a flower shop to London's highest-rated burger joint. But here's what gets me excited about SS 2.0. This is just the beginning. My software engineering background is finally fusing with everything we've learned in hospitality. We're using technology to solve every pain point we lived through. Even building custom AI agents to level up our customer service even further. Because the moment you stop improving is the moment someone else passes you.

8am on a bank holiday Monday. Me, a coffee, and 50 ethernet cables I had no idea how to install. Welcome to SS 2.0. I'm installing structured cabling for our new kiosk systems at Simply Smashed. First time in my life doing anything like this. "What's a patch panel?" I asked ChatGPT at 8:17am. "How do you terminate Cat6 cables?" at 9:43am. "Why is nothing working?" at 11:22am. By 2pm, I had a fully functioning network infrastructure I'd built from scratch. Here's what hit me: AI has brought back my joy of learning. Not the forced, academic way that killed my appetite in school. The way I actually learn best - by doing, by building, by solving real problems. People always say "I need to learn AI" or "I should learn coding" but never start. Here's why: They're trying to learn a field, not solve a problem. Want to actually learn something? Don't pick a subject. Pick an outcome. I didn't set out to learn structured cabling. I set out to install kiosks that'll transform our customer experience. The cabling knowledge was just what I needed to get there. Every skill I've gained building Simply Smashed came this way. Not from courses or textbooks, but from having something I desperately wanted to build. And now with AI as my personal tutor? I can learn anything I need, exactly when I need it. The builder in me isn't just back. It's supercharged. This is just the beginning of SS 2.0. So much more coming.

Why we're closing our restaurant for the first week of Ramadan... And why it'll cost us 30% of our monthly revenue: Most restaurants are rushing to capitalize on Iftar sales right now. We're doing the opposite. At Simply Smashed, we've made it a tradition to close during Ramadan's first week. Here's why: Iftar service is brutal. Imagine 50+ concurrent orders hitting simultaneously, all made fresh to order. Our team works incredibly hard during this month, managing both their fasts and intense service periods. So we give them this time to: • Reset mentally • Connect with family • Focus on their spiritual journey But we don't stop there. Throughout Ramadan, we only open an hour before Iftar. No daytime operations. No pressure on our fasting staff. These decisions cost us about 20-30% of our usual monthly revenue. But you know what? Values > Profits. I've worked through many Ramadans before starting this business. I know how challenging it can be to balance work and worship during this sacred month. That's why, as we've grown, we've intentionally built these accommodations into our business model. It might not be what maximizes profit. But it maximizes barakah (blessing). And that's the foundation we're building on. ↓ If you're interested in learning more about how we're building a values-first business, follow me for regular insights on ethical entrepreneurship.

The UK has a prayer space problem—and we've all felt it. Many restaurants market iftar deals for Ramadan, but forget the most important part—a place to pray. Picture this: You're out for iftar. The restaurant's packed with Muslims breaking their fast. Maghrib time comes... but there's nowhere to pray. And it's not just Ramadan. Mosques closed between jama'ah. Tight salah windows in winter. Sisters left with even fewer options. We can do better. We must do better. That's why at Simply Smashed, prayer spaces have been available since we first opened our doors. Last month, we made it our pledge that every future Simply Smashed location will have a dedicated place to pray. Every Simply Smashed location offers a place to pray—brothers and sisters alike. Just ask our staff, and we'll make it happen. And here's the key part: You don't have to be a customer. If you need to pray, our doors are open for you. We know mosques are doing their best. Many are donation-based and rely on volunteers, making it difficult to stay open all day. That's where businesses like ours can step in to help fill the gaps. This is about more than burgers. We're committed to making prayer spaces available everywhere we grow: • Every Simply Smashed location has dedicated prayer facilities, alhamdulillah • We ensure both brothers and sisters have equal, dignified spaces • Our staff are trained to help facilitate prayer space access • Prayer mats are always available and clean No Muslim should have to miss salah or pray in a car park because they couldn't find a space. No sister should feel anxious about where she'll pray Asr during a shopping trip. No one should have to choose between breaking their fast at a restaurant and making maghrib prayer on time. This is our open prayer policy. But our vision goes beyond us. Imagine a network of accessible prayer spaces across the UK—cafés, restaurants, and businesses creating solutions for the community. This is our step forward, and we hope it inspires others to join us. We build with barakah, and we're proud to serve our community in more ways than one. Check us out at Simply Smashed and follow along as we continue building with barakah 🙏🏾

We ban men from eating at our restaurant. Well, on Sisters’ Nights, at least. At Simply Smashed, our Sisters’ Nights are one-of-a-kind: exclusive evenings where only women are allowed to eat in-store. These nights are about more than just food. They create a safe, welcoming space for women to relax, connect, and enjoy themselves. Our most recent Sisters’ Night was a collaboration with Shabbir Hassan’s Faith Space, where we hosted a Palestinian-themed evening. Faith Space brought in Palestinian speakers to share their stories, and 50% of the night’s proceeds were donated to Human Aid & Advocacy’s Gaza Appeal. Initiatives like these tie directly into the larger mission of Simply Smashed: elevating the standards of Muslim entrepreneurship. Why do we do things like Sisters’ Nights? Because the best way to inspire change isn’t by telling others what to do—it’s by leading with action. Since launching Sisters’ Nights, we’ve already seen other restaurants follow the trend and host their own versions. And that’s the goal. To show that initiatives like these are not only meaningful but commercially viable. And if they’re commercially viable, you’ll see other businesses follow—something we know all too well in the Muslim food industry. This is part of our wider approach of building with barakah and injecting creativity to inspire others. It’s about setting trends that strengthen our communities and create lasting change. If you’ve been to one of our Sisters’ Nights, we’d love to hear your thoughts. And if not—keep an eye out for the next one. PS: What do you think of the banner? Can anyone guess which brand I got inspiration from for the copy? (Hint: It’s from a chocolate.)

The landlord had one requirement: sell beer. We said no and left. A while back, I was standing inside this perfect empty pub thinking about everything we could build there. 18 months it had been sitting vacant. Dust on the windows, chairs stacked on tables, that sad emptiness of a place where people used to gather. But I could see it transformed: families sharing smash burgers where bar stools used to be, kids laughing where drunk arguments once happened, our punching machine where kegs used to sit - people competing to beat the high score instead of drowning their sorrows. The space was perfect. The rent was reasonable. The location had everything we needed. Then the landlord restrictions hit us like a cold slap. Heineken owns the building. Every tenant must sell beer on the premises. No exceptions. For our halal concept, that's not just impossible - it goes against everything we stand for. I felt that familiar knot in my stomach. The same one I get when people suggest we "just add a few non-halal options" to capture more customers. This wasn't about finding a loophole. This was about a company stuck in 1995 trying to force 2025 businesses into their dying model. Here's what most people don't understand: since 2000, the UK has lost 15,800 pubs. That's 35% of them completely gone. Last year alone, 490 more closed permanently. This isn't random bad luck. This is what happens when you build your entire business model around something people increasingly don't want. Meanwhile, we're building spaces where everyone belongs. Where great food brings people together instead of alcohol dividing them. Where a Muslim family and their non-Muslim neighbors can share the same table without anyone feeling excluded. That empty pub sitting there for 18 months? Perfect metaphor for what happens when you refuse to evolve. I walked out feeling disappointed for exactly two hours. Then I realized something: Heineken's inflexibility just saved us from partnering with a company that fundamentally doesn't understand the future we're building. We're not just opening restaurants. We're proving that the old model of social spaces - built around exclusion, centered on alcohol, designed for a narrow demographic - is finished. Every time an established player tells us our approach won't work, the market proves them wrong. Every time someone says we're being too restrictive by staying halal, our customers show us the opposite: they're hungry for spaces that don't require them to compromise their values. The same family obsession with perfection that saved us during COVID. That perfect location is still out there somewhere. When we find it, the landlord will understand what we're building instead of trying to force us into their expired playbook. Sometimes the best opportunities come disguised as closed doors. This one just reminded us why we're building something completely different.

We got review bombed for supporting Palestine, so we doubled down - now we're UK's #1 rated burger joint. I remember when we first started getting review-bombed. One-star reviews started trickling in. No comments, just stars. Then we saw the pattern: People targeting us because we chose to stock Salam Cola (which donates 10% to Palestine) over mainstream alternatives. Their message was clear: "The food industry shouldn't be involved in politics." But here's what they didn't understand: When your entire supply chain shares your values (from butchers to distributors), and your customer base shares your values, the only thing silencing you is yourself. So we decided to flip the script. Within 4 days, we: • Launched a special burger campaign • Partnered with Muslim Aid UK • Donated 100% of profits to Gaza • Doubled down on our partnership with Salaam Cola France The result? Over £4,000 raised in just one week. But more importantly, our community rallied behind us with thousands of genuine 5-star reviews. This taught me something profound about business: Many Muslim business owners operate from fear: • Fear of standing out • Fear of rocking the boat • Fear of losing customers But here's the truth: If your values align with your community, standing firm only makes you stronger. That's why Simply Smashed isn't just a burger joint. We're setting a new standard for Muslim businesses: • Prayer rooms in our restaurant • Sisters-only dining nights • Quran recitation in our content • Unapologetic support for causes we believe in The best part? Other restaurants are following suit. Because the best way to change an industry isn't through force. It's by showing there's a better way. ↓ If you enjoyed this, follow me for more insights on building value-driven businesses.

"You're the Palestinian burger guy, right?" 8 hours of interrogation. That's how I knew we were onto something. Three weeks ago, Ibrahim Javed and I tried to cross into the West Bank. Routine questions became an 8-hour detention. Separated rooms. Aggressive searches. They'd found our Simply Smashed campaigns, Palestine flags, Gaza fundraising, everything we thought was "just charity work from a burger joint." Then the interrogator snapped. Started hurling abuse. Told me to "get the f*** out of his country." Here's the thing: He cracked. I didn't. Ibrahim and I walked out and burst into laughter. Not from humour but from validation. They'd just proven our "small" actions had real impact. When charity drives from a burger joint trigger 8-hour government detention? Your "small" actions aren't small at all. Every campaign compounds. Every stand creates ripples they can't ignore. But here's what happened next: Still processing our rejection, Ibrahim and I immediately started talking solutions. Technical platforms for community organizing. Tools to counter systemic discrimination. Solutions to address what we'd just experienced firsthand. The same system that spent 8 hours trying to discourage us accidentally energized us to build even more. Two builders, detained for what they called "small" activism, walking away planning solutions that weren't small at all. That's when it hit me: We spend years perfecting our craft. Chasing ARR. Building unicorns for investors. But our communities don't need more donated profit margins. They need builders using their skills where it matters most. The same product thinking that scales startups? It can scale justice. That's why I'm proud to support the team running Deen Developers's Hack for Gaza. Because the best validation isn't an 8-hour interrogation. It's building solutions so powerful they make interrogations irrelevant. Your skills are your superpower. Time to use them. Join us. Link in comments. ⬇️

These teenage brothers just recited the entire Quran from memory in 9 hours - finishing just 2 seconds apart. Here's why their story matters to our entire community: At dawn, Abdurrahman (15) and Saabiq (16) began their extraordinary challenge. Hour after hour, verse after verse, they raced through 6,236 verses purely from memory. By 4:30pm, they had achieved what takes most people years to accomplish. Their father walked through our doors, eyes gleaming with joy, his sons' achievement radiating through his proud smile. We've partnered with Quran Revision Project - Europe's largest gathering of Huffadh - for our Road to Ramadan campaign, offering free meals to these dedicated memorizers of the Quran. But this isn't just about food. It's about recognition. It's about saying: "We see you." Our Huffadh represent something profound in our community: The preservation of our heritage. The bridge between generations. The future of our spiritual leadership. Yet too often, these young champions go unrecognized: • Years of dawn-to-dusk dedication • Sacrificing typical teenage experiences • Balancing intense memorization with school • Carrying the weight of religious responsibility at such a young age This Ramadan, they'll lead Taraweeh prayers at their local mosque in Barking. Think about that - at 15 and 16, they'll guide hundreds in prayer. At Simply Smashed, we believe business isn't just about transactions. It's about strengthening the fabric of our community. It's about creating spaces where achievements like these are celebrated. Where young people feel seen, valued, and supported. Because when we uplift our youth, we elevate our entire community. When we celebrate their dedication, we inspire the next generation. When we show them we're proud, we give them the strength to continue. ↓ This Ramadan, let's commit to appreciating our Huffadh more. They're not just memorizing text - they're preserving our heritage, one verse at a time. Share this to show our young Huffadh: Your community stands with you. We see you. And we are incredibly proud.

This weekend, I’ve been building something I’ve dreamed about for years. Young Muslims face so much emotionally, especially during their teenage years. Some of us were lucky to have an "Ameen" in our lives. That person in the prayer room who gave the right advice at the right time. But many didn’t have that privilege. So I built Ameen, your Muslim companion. Ameen provides comfort, shares relevant duas, and offers lessons from the Seerah. It’s not about fatwas or rulings—it’s about support when it’s needed most. I spent the weekend rapidly prototyping and shipped an MVP (check comments). It’s simple, not perfect, but that’s the point. The goal is to iterate quickly, collect feedback, and build something that genuinely resonates with its users. This same product thinking is what built Simply Smashed into the UK’s highest-rated burger joint. From data-driven menu designs to understanding what our community values most, product thinking has always been central to what I do. Even though Simply Smashed keeps me busy, I’ve missed building products like this. It’s about identifying a problem, understanding the user, and delivering value fast. Also, I’ve also been expanding my design skills as a product manager. Ameen has been a great way to put that into practice and push myself creatively while solving meaningful problems. Accuracy will get better but check it out now in the comments, what do you think?

Yes. I am the face of that meme you see every Ramadan... The story of how my face became a global Muslim internet phenomenon: I'm that guy from the "When you're fasting but..." meme. You know, the one that resurfaces every single Ramadan across multiple countries. One of the wildest moments? Standing in line for Fajr prayer and seeing someone scrolling through that meme on their phone. Right next to me. The story behind it is pretty simple: I made a joke post when I was 15. Not even based on real experience - just something my friend and I thought would be funny. But it took on a life of its own. The meme has been translated into languages I can't even read. It's been remixed into marriage posts (because Muslim Twitter always finds a way). People have twisted it, turned it, and transformed it into their own versions. Every Ramadan, without fail, it comes back in new forms. Screenshots, reposts, tags - crossing cultural and language barriers I never imagined. At first, I wasn't sure how to feel about being an international meme. Then I had a realization: If life gives you viral memes, use them. So we recreated the entire meme inside Simply Smashed, our restaurant. Complete with my dad in the shot (yes, he's a good sport). Sometimes your biggest "embarrassments" can become opportunities. You just have to lean into them. ↓ If you enjoyed this story, follow me for more insights on building a brand that stands out (even if it starts with becoming a global meme phenomenon).

I once hired a Boris bike to deliver a missing chicken burger to a customer's front door. He grabbed the bag, and shut the door without a word. We were mid-rush at Simply Smashed, maybe a Friday night, orders stacking up on the UberEats tablet. I checked a bag going out and realised we'd missed an item. Chicken burger, already paid for, already on its way to someone's house minus the thing they actually wanted. So I called the customer. Got the address. It was like a 5 minute cycle away. I ran outside, tapped a Boris bike, put the bag in the basket and just started pedalling through Whitechapel. Got there, knocked on the door, slightly out of breath. The guy opens it, looks at the bag, takes it, and closes the door. No thank you, no eye contact, nothing. I stood there for a second like... cool. Then I cycled back to the shop and got on with service. The thing is, I'm not telling this story because the guy was rude. He probably didn't even clock what just happened. He ordered food, food arrived, life continued. That's honestly fair enough. I'm telling it because that's what the early days of building anything actually feel like. You sprint to solve a problem nobody asked you to sprint for. You over-deliver by a stupid amount. And the response is silence. The guy didn't leave a review. He definitely didn't sign up for a loyalty program. I'm fairly sure he didn't even realise the founder just personally cycled a chicken burger to his door. Just a closed door and a Boris bike to return. And you go back and do it again the next night because that's the job. The gap between what you put in and what you get back is enormous when you're starting out. You have to be okay with that gap or you won't survive it.

I've left Simply Smashed. After 2 years of building the highest rated burger joint in London, I'm stepping back. My brother's taking over day-to-day. I'm building something new. It's strange to write that. This was never supposed to be my thing. My dad has been in the food industry for over 35 years. Started in a tiny French seaside town called Dieppe where it felt like we were the only asian family around, been doing this since before I was born. The restaurant was always his world. Then my parents got on a flight to Bangladesh and lockdown got announced mid-air. Me and my brother suddenly had a restaurant with no customers, staff who needed paying, and rent that didn't care about pandemics. We ran the Help Our Heroes campaign, delivered thousands of pizza slices to hospitals across London, kept the lights on for months. When we started thinking about selling, a buyer came in and made my dad feel like a fool. Said we were "bleeding out." Made a lowball offer so insulting my dad slammed the table and walked out. They just smirked and lit cigarettes outside. That led to a chain of events which led up to starting Simply Smashed. We launched three concepts at once. Simply Smashed just happened to be the one that took off. A £100 grill. Tables pushed away. The front space rented to a flower shop so people walked through flowers to pick up their burgers. We had no money to do it properly so we just told people what we were building and let them watch us figure it out. Today we're rated 4.9 stars. The highest rated burger joint in London. Looking back now it's hard to separate Simply Smashed from my family. My dad showing up every single time we needed him. My brother building operations that actually worked. My sister-in-law who created half the recipes we still serve today. We got review bombed for stocking Salaam Cola and the community showed up for us. Grateful for all of it. This was always a family thing. It still is. My brother has been with us from early and I trust him completely to take Simply Smashed and Peruvian Street Kitchen forward. I'm not disappearing - I'll still be around for strategic oversight. But the day-to-day is his now. Excited to see where he takes them both. I'm building something new. Can't say much yet but if you followed the Simply Smashed journey, you know the playbook. More soon iA.

There's this lunch from my Goldman days I can't get out of my head. After 16 failed attempts, I finally nailed the green sauce that had senior bankers queuing in Savile Row suits. Here's why I spent 2 months obsessing over chicken: There was this Peruvian place near our…

I'm building @PSK_UKI because I want to bring some new flavours to the halal food scene with simply smashed it was about entering a saturated market (smashed burgers everywhere) and trying to rise above with peruvian street kitchen it's about introducing something new & fresh!

Proud to announce our newest food brand @PSK_UKI I’m building the most addictive chicken and rice box in the city. Slow-cooked Peruvian grilled chicken with our super addictive green sauce. Think Shah’s Halal but Peruvian. Peruvian Street Kitchen launches October 2025.

Left photo: Our first PSK box. Leftover chicken and rice. Right photo: What 2 months of obsession creates. Most founders would hide that first photo. But here's what tech taught me that most restaurants don't understand: You can't iterate on an idea. You can only iterate on something that exists. Version 1 was literally leftovers from my fridge. Air fryer chicken. Yesterday's rice. Some of our Peruvian Thigh green sauce drizzled on top. It wasn't good. But it existed. And once something exists, you can make it better. Tested 8 different rices at home. Built 3 sauces that work like a team. Tweaked the char, the steam, the ratios. Ate it every single day for 2 months straight. This is why our second kitchen has stickers we slapped up ourselves instead of fancy banners. Why we're testing in plastic containers before designing packaging. Because perfection is a direction, not a starting point. Most restaurants spend months planning the perfect menu. We shipped ugly and improved daily. Two months later, I'm still not bored of eating this. That's when you know you've built something dangerous. PSK - Peruvian Street Kitchen. Launching this week. From leftover chicken to London's next obsession. Magic doesn't appear. It evolves.
First look of Peruvian Street Kitchen!

Someone spent £100 trying to sabotage my stealth launch. And honestly? It's hilarious. So we're quietly testing PSK (Peruvian Street Kitchen). Not advertising. Just fulfilling random orders. Day 1: This guy orders from Simply Smashed. We go all out - extra portions, made with love, the works. Check the app that night: 1 star. Day 2: SAME GUY orders from PSK. Wait. We're in stealth mode. How did he even find both brands? Whatever. We try even harder. Make it perfect. That night: Another 1 star. Then the smoking gun: Someone left a 1-star Google review. On our brand new listing. Two hours after I created it. We hadn't even taken a single order yet. That's when I knew. This wasn't about the food. After that, this guy starts trying to order from BOTH brands. Every. Single. Day. Since leaving those 1-star reviews, he's attempted nearly £100 worth of orders. We just keep rejecting them. The Uber Eats account manager was like "yeah you can just ban him" so casually. Like this happens all the time. Because it does. The food business is weirdly tribal. There's literally takeaway wars happening up north right now. Actual wars. Over chicken shops. When I first started Simply Smashed, this stuff destroyed me. I'd see a fake review and spiral. Question everything. Lose sleep wondering what I did wrong. Check the reviews obsessively. Let it consume my whole day. My confidence would shatter. I'd second-guess every decision. Now? I recognise the pattern immediately. Competitor sees you doing well. Competitor panics. Competitor attacks. It's actually validation. Someone is SO pressed about our quiet little test that they're burning their own money AND time stalking our Google listings. The shift happened when I realised: You can't control the tribal nonsense. You can only control the food you make and how you treat real customers. Their panic is just noise. Your focus is the signal. These days when I see this behaviour, I don't spiral. I smile. Because if someone's willing to spend £100 trying to stop you... You must be doing something right. Anyway, we're thinking of adding him to our loyalty programme. At this rate, he'll get a free meal by Tuesday.

A dad tried to buy chicken and rice from me 5 times in one week. We were closed every single time. His son had spotted PSK on my Twitter. Said it was "better than Shah's and Pepe's." In their house, that's high praise. See, this father and son talk about everything. Football. Work. Life. But especially food. It's their language. So when the son mentioned this new spot just around the corner from their house, the dad made a mental note. Monday: Walked over. Closed. Tuesday: Tried again. Closed. Wednesday: Third attempt. Still closed. Thursday: Fourth time. Nothing. Each time he went home empty-handed. Each time he could've given up. Any other dad orders Deliveroo. Moves on. Not this one. Friday, attempt number five. He sees our gate open. Walks up to the building - door open. Reaches our kitchen door. Lights on inside. "Are you actually open? Can I buy food?" We'd been operating limited hours. Testing. Perfecting. Missing customers like him all week. Here's where it gets worse: we'd just sold our last portion. Fresh batch would take 30 minutes. I told him straight. Expected him to leave. "I'll wait. I'm not going home empty-handed." So he waited. In our little kitchen. Watching us prep. 30 minutes later, he left with two boxes. One for his son. One for himself. That night, a father and son connected over chicken and rice. Here's the thing: No one should have to try 5 times to taste what we're building. That's why on November 2nd, PSK is doing a one-day pop-up at Simply Smashed Stepney. One day. Full menu. Three sauces. The chicken and rice that's about to change London's lunch game. No more closed doors. No more missed connections. No more "we just ran out." Just the most addictive chicken and rice box you've ever had. November 2nd. Simply Smashed Stepney. Come see what that father waited for. Come taste what London's been missing.

Running burgers and rice boxes from the same kitchen is absolute chaos. Found that out the hard way yesterday. PSK's first pop-up. Simply Smashed still firing orders. Two brands, one kitchen, complete madness at 2pm. We opened an hour late. People waited. Nobody left. Once we found our flow though? Different story. Orders flying out. Both brands running smooth. The team locked in. Then we sold out an hour early. Despite overstocking by 40%. I've been personally messaging everyone who came. The responses are keeping me up: "Never going Shah's again" "1000/10 - just regret not ordering more" "Let me know if we can invest" That last one got me. Two weeks ago PSK was just an idea. Yesterday someone wanted to invest. My mum's still handmaking our sauces. Every batch. Won't let anyone else touch them yet. That's how we build brands. With our own hands first. Learning every detail. Every process. Every standard. Running multiple brands from one kitchen isn't new for us. But when both are firing at full speed? That's when you really feel it. The pressure. The energy. The buzz when it all clicks. This week, we announce PSK's first permanent location. The chaos was worth it though. Every single second. Because those messages? That's what makes all the behind-the-scenes work worth it. London - thank you for waiting that extra hour. Thank you for believing in what we're building.

I've been lying to you. Every time you saw me at Simply Smashed, there was something I wasn't telling you. For the last two years while I was running the restaurant, I was also advising Series A founders on their content strategy. Part time, on the side, mostly in secret. I was on calls with YC founders and A16z portfolio companies, founders building companies that will be household names in five years. And I was taking those calls from my restaurant. There's this memory I keep coming back to. I'm on a call with a founder talking positioning, narrative strategy, how to become the voice of their space. Elite player. The kind of person you'd expect to be advising from some nice office somewhere. And I'm standing next to our Simply Smashed punching machine. I had to be on site that day. Couldn't leave. So I just found a corner, put my noise-cancelling headphones on, and took the call anyway. My resume said: Restaurant Owner. My calendar said: Strategy Call with a16z Portfolio Company. They had no idea where I was. Most people didn't know I was doing this at all. Here's how that even happened. When Simply Smashed took off, people started asking how we did it. Highest rated burger joint in London with no marketing budget. Pure organic storytelling. My brother saw it before I did. He introduced me to someone at a content strategy agency - the kind that works with YC founders and a16z portfolio companies. They were looking for someone. My brother knew this was exactly what I'd been doing without realising it. That someone was Mustafa Khan, ACA. Who would end up becoming my co-founder. I said yes immediately. Everything I'd learned at Simply Smashed was from first principles. Pure instinct. I wanted to see what this looked like at scale with the smartest founders in the world. That became my arena. I started advising founders. Got them over 25M+ views across X and LinkedIn Then I got promoted to Head of Training. Responsible for training writers and creative directors on how to do what I'd been doing on gut feel alone. And it fit like a glove. Looking back, the thread was always there. Every project I've ever worked on grew through storytelling. I just didn't have words for what I was doing. It was instinct compounding over years. Last year I left the agency with Mustafa. We're building Draper. AI agents plus human taste for founder storytelling. Same instinct that's been compounding this whole time. Same playbook that took a burger joint to number one. Now we're helping other founders do it for their companies. we've been cooking like crazy btw. can't wait to share more.

I built the highest rated burger joint in London. 4.9 stars, 3000+ reviews. Those two years taught me more about building than any MBA ever could. The thing about the food industry is nothing is theoretical. From day one you're making decisions with real money on razor thin margins. One bad weekend and you feel it in your bank account by Friday, not next quarter. → We got burgled → I dealt with literal fires → One supplier issue and the whole menu changes overnight → I had staff not show up while I was two hours away with no way to get back → You learn to read people very quickly because you genuinely don't have time not to Simply Smashed started from a kitchen we were already using and maybe £100 on a new grill. That was the entire business plan. When every pound counts you develop this instinct for what's worth spending on and what isn't. That instinct doesn't go away when you move into tech. It just gets applied differently. Every decision I make building Draper now, whether it's hiring, spending, prioritising, I can trace back to something I learned in that kitchen. That's not from a textbook, it's from a Friday night that went sideways. And honestly I'd take someone who's survived a Friday night service with half their staff missing over someone who's only ever seen pressure in a case study. It's the most expensive MBA that I never paid for tbh

I was building an AI company between burger orders and honestly I miss it. I keep looking at this photo and it's kinda crazy. Simply Smashed was on its second location. Peruvian Street Kitchen was on its first. And somewhere in between both of those I decided this was also where I'd start building an AI content company on Replit. I had my laptop wedged into whatever corner I could find, squinting at code I barely understood while delivery drivers walked in and out. I'd be mid-prompt and someone would shout that orders were backing up so I'd get stuck in packing rice boxes and saucing them up. Then come back to my laptop trying to remember what I was even building. If the rush got too much the laptop just got closed and that was that. I'd been training writers at a ghostwriting agency and I could see so clearly that the whole industry was about to flip. Like I could literally feel it. And I had this thing in my head going if I don't start building this right now, from this kitchen, on this dying laptop, someone else is going to do it and I'll be watching from behind a fryer. It wasn't a plan btw. I didn't sit down and map anything out. Two food brands running, a kitchen that's too small for any of this, and my brain just going "yeah but what if we also built a tech company from here." I physically couldn't not do it. That was a couple of months ago. Draper is now past ramen profitable and growing every month. Peruvian Street Kitchen is opening its second physical location soon iA. Everything is better now. Better setup, better tools, actual laptops that work. But I keep coming back to this photo because something about building from that kitchen felt different and I can't fully explain why. P.S: I'm a firm believer that being in the trenches means delaying your trim, you have to earn it as a reward.

Content is product. Product is content. I've said it maybe 200 times now. Most founders nod and then go do the opposite anyway. We ran Simply Smashed with zero paid marketing. Literally zero. We were just documenting the messiness of building a burger joint from the back of a flower shop and posting it, and that was doing the job a £5k/month ad budget would've done. We became the highest-rated burger spot in London and never boosted a single post. Then MiniDeed happened. The product was good and the impact was real and nobody knew it existed. The thing about having no distribution is it doesn't matter how good your product is. Nobody sees it. Completely opposite outcomes that somehow taught me the exact same thing. The founders who get this are building content into the product from day one. The GTM isn't a department you bolt on in month six, it's the whole thing. If you just raised and you're trying to decide whether to invest in content or put it off, the thing you're actually deferring is distribution.

Let's address the elephant in the room - most AI content is garbage. Here’s why: LLMs copying from other LLM generated articles. Repurposed slop from Reddit dressed up as insights. You can feel it when you're scrolling. It all sounds the same. But here's what I've learned about content that actually works after working with YC and A16z founders. When Simply Smashed took off, it wasn't because we posted more than anyone else. It was because we told our story. In our voice. People could feel the difference. That's why they kept showing up. The founders I worked with who won - same thing. Their story, told properly, compounding over time. The thing is, most founders don't have time for this. They're building. You can't cook with one hand on a phone trying to document yourself. You need both hands in the work. That's what me and Mustafa kept talking about. Builders should be focused on building. AI should be documenting you cooking. That's what we're building with Draper. Right now the human taste is us. We work with founders closely to get their voice right. But we're codifying what we've learned into systems. The vision is the human taste becomes you. Your stories. Your voice. The way you actually talk. Not repurposed slop. But actual authentic human stories that's told at scale. Right now we're deep in LinkedIn. But the vision is bigger. Content engines for entire teams, not just founders. Content marketing is shifting on how companies attract customers, investors and talent (will share more on this soon). We're building the infrastructure to make it scalable. we've been heads down cooking too. finally got some time to pull out the phone. lots to come, more soon.

I've been using AI wrong this whole time. For months, I tried getting it to create viral food photos for our burger joint. It kept spitting out fake-looking garbage with weird textures and plastic-looking elements. Then I realised something that changed everything. Instead of asking AI to replace my work, I started using it as my editing coach. I upload my real burger photos to ChatGPT and say: "Help me make this pop." It gives me specific tips: adjust the shadows under the patty, boost the saturation on the lettuce, sharpen the bacon edges. My first result? A Wagyu Bacon Burger that looked like actual food porn instead of AI slop. But here's where it gets interesting. This "AI as coach" philosophy is now how we're starting to operate across everything. We feed our 2850+ Google reviews (4.9 stars) into AI systems that analyses patterns invisible to human eyes. Then it coaches our front-of-house team with surgical precision. Not replacing our people. Making them superhuman at reading customer needs. The insight that changed everything: AI isn't good at creating. It's incredible at teaching. It can't make a perfect burger photo, but it can teach you to see light and composition like a pro photographer. It can't serve customers, but it can turn your team into service ninjas by analysing thousands of data points you'd never notice. We're not just London's highest-rated burger joint anymore. We're staying there because we learned the difference between automation and elevation.

We 2x'd our deep work without adding a single hour to the week. it's the best thing we've done for Draper and it cost us literally nothing. Mustafa brought this from his old agency. When he first suggested it I remember thinking it was a bit rigid but we tried it anyway and honestly it changed how we work completely. → Monday and Wednesday: all client calls, stacked back to back → Tuesday, Thursday, Friday: just building That's it. (revolutionary stuff I know) The thing is most founders think they have a time problem. They don't. They have a transition problem. That Gen Z meme where someone books two hours before a meeting to stress about it and one hour after to recover is funny because it's basically true. The actual work takes 15 minutes but the mental commute between tasks eats the rest of your day. A 15 minute task that felt impossible at 3pm just flows on a quiet Tuesday morning. So we stopped trying to manage it and just stacked everything. six months in and honestly I don't think we could go back.

I think we need to talk about this because it's gotten quite bad. I'm the leg. Mustafa's the arm. Together we're one person on Zoom. Every time I screen share my Chrome crashes. And every time Mustafa turns his camera on his laptop just dies. So we've developed this system where we both cover for each other. He shares screen, I keep my camera on, and we both talk through our sections. Between us we've got one working laptop and we've just accepted it as normal operations at this point. We were on a call the other day and I froze on screen mid-sentence. Mustafa just goes "yeah this happens whenever he shares his screen, his laptop crashes and my camera crashes. So like it's an arm and a leg." Then casually explained our whole system to the person on the call like he was describing how we make coffee in the morning. The guy just started laughing. We're an AI content startup btw. We talk about technology all day. And we can't run Google Meet on one machine without it catching fire. (the irony is not lost on us) One of the founders we work with found out and went full big brother on us. "Get the Pro. Don't get the Air. The Air doesn't even have a fan." Didn't even wait for a response. Just told us what to order like he'd been through it himself and wasn't letting us make the same mistake. Fair enough honestly. We ordered two M4 Pros that same day. They arrive in about a month because of the chip shortage. Prices have gone up too. So we're paying more to wait longer to be able to do our jobs properly. Cool. Everyone thinks early stage startups look like the pitch deck. Clean. Intentional. Two co-founders who've got it sorted. Behind the scenes your hardware is failing and your processes are held together by habits you invented out of desperation. And somehow they still say "that was a great call" at the end. oh btw - we should be fully operational humans by April. probably.

I keep entering domains the slow way in the fastest era in history. Twice now and I'd do it again. You can go to Claude right now and start building in a domain you have zero expertise in. And it might work tbh, in fact, we're in the most competitive era of software in history because of that. So why would you go into a domain you haven't earned? Go into the one where you've put the most reps in. That's your edge now. We grew Simply Smashed to the highest rated burger in London organically and that whole experience pulled me into writing for founders at agencies. I did that for a year, which led to Draper. With Vibenasheeds same thing. Grew a YouTube channel first, figured out what hit and what didn't, then started building. It reminds me of something Abdel once said to me... AI gets you 60% of the way there, it's on you to fill the gap. That 60% is everything that's ever been publicly scraped. The other 40% doesn't exist in any dataset. You learn it in the arena. P.S: If you want a break from the arena Kotor (it's like a less busy lake como) is one of the most underrated places in Europe, definitely recommend :) .

Every Muslim creator faces the same impossible choice. Use mainstream beats that compromise your values, or create content in silence. I felt this firsthand running Simply Smashed. We had a strict no-music policy, but how do you create engaging content without sound? How do you build atmosphere in your restaurant when customers walk in? I tried everything. Different beats, different ambient sounds. Nothing quite fit the vibe I wanted. Eventually we settled on live sports in the background - it worked for the restaurant atmosphere. But the content problem remained unsolved. That's when I remembered my old fascination with vocal beats. What started as casual interest became urgent necessity. So I taught myself. Every single night after brutal restaurant shifts, I'd come home exhausted and spend 1-2 hours learning to craft beats. My fingers fumbling through software I barely understood. My ears slowly training to hear what worked. Seven weeks in, something clicked. My YouTube channel "Lofi Muslim" hit 130 subscribers. I'm averaging 300 views daily. Comments started flooding in from Saudi Arabia, France from creators across continents saying "Finally, something that fits." Then came the moment that changed everything. A complete stranger bought my first beat. I stared at that notification for minutes. Someone I'd never met just paid for something I created in my bedroom after a restaurant shift. That's when I realised this wasn't just solving my problem. Muslim creators everywhere are starving for options. They're compromising their values because quality alternatives barely exist. Now I've got beats on Spotify and Apple Music. Creators are using my work in their content without me doing any marketing. The beat store is growing. But here's what really gets me: In an era where we consume endlessly, building something people actually want feels revolutionary. Lmk what you think! Do you vibe with the beats? Link in the comments.

Side project of the week: I built an AI that composes music and then removes the music from itself. vibenasheeds: the claude for making vocal nasheed beats. Some of you might remember the lofi Muslim YouTube channel I posted about last year. I was making nasheed beats after 12-hour shifts at Simply Smashed because I could not find halal background music. Every nasheed pack was either £30+ per beat or so rinsed that you'd hear the same track in three different Muslim creators' videos on the same day. That whole channel was a test run... I've been cooking this up quietly between everything else. vibenasheeds is the actual thing. You prompt the vibe you want for your scene and AI generates a full track from scratch. Then what I'm calling the halal engine kicks in and separates the stems and strips the instruments out of the file, gone. What's left is vocals and daf. It composes with instruments first because that's how you get something that actually sounds good, then removes them... sounds like a weird extra step but the output is better (and I spent an embarrassing amount of time looking). The thing about the nasheed scene right now is the creators in it are incredible. I grew up watching them figure out an entire genre from scratch with basically nothing. You ever watch Chris Howett cycling through the mountains of Switzerland on an electric scooter? Half of why that youtube content hits the way it does is the audio. Muslim creators have been locked out of that entire dimension, you're either using the same 50 beats as everyone else or you're working in silence and hoping the visuals carry it. I want to describe what I'm hearing in my head for a specific moment and have it exist. Link in comments to try it out!

Fear of God's Essentials hoodie retails at £180. I built one that beat their fabric specs for £60. It sold out in 3 hours. The product isn't why it sold out though. The storytelling is. So here's how that even happened. I went to Bangladesh and spent time studying how the supply chains behind brands like Fear of God actually work on the ground. I started building SIMPLYCLO from there. Our hoodie came in at 364 GSM, Fear of God's Essentials sits at 347. We were using the same factories in the same country with better fabric weight at a third of the price. None of that honestly matters if nobody knows you exist. So I documented the whole thing. I posted the factory visits, the fabric sourcing, ran brand name polls on Twitter, made TikToks from Bangladesh showing the entire process. Every single decision was made in public. Someone in Selfridges recognised the hoodie on me five weeks after we conceived the brand and said they'd already heard of it. We hadn't spent anything on ads or PR, it was all just content. It sold out in 3 hours. People had watched the whole story unfold in real time and by the time the hoodie dropped they felt like they were part of it. That's what actually moved units, not the GSM. SIMPLYCLO was a passion project and honestly one of the most fun things I've ever built. I ended up closing it down, but the thesis stuck with me. Content was the entire go-to-market. I just documented the build and let people in instead of spending anything on ads or PR.

Here's why their story matters to our entire community: At dawn, Abdurrahman (15) and Saabiq (16) began their extraordinary challenge. Hour after hour, verse after verse, they raced through 6,236 verses purely from memory. By 4:30pm, they had achieved what takes most people years to accomplish. Their father walked through our doors, eyes gleaming with joy, his sons' achievement radiating through his proud smile. We've partnered with Quran Revision Project - Europe's largest gathering of Huffadh - for our Road to Ramadan campaign, offering free meals to these dedicated memorizers of the Quran. But this isn't just about food. It's about recognition. It's about saying: "We see you." Our Huffadh represent something profound in our community: The preservation of our heritage. The bridge between generations. The future of our spiritual leadership. Yet too often, these young champions go unrecognized: • Years of dawn-to-dusk dedication • Sacrificing typical teenage experiences • Balancing intense memorization with school • Carrying the weight of religious responsibility at such a young age This Ramadan, they'll lead Taraweeh prayers at their local mosque in Barking. Think about that - at 15 and 16, they'll guide hundreds in prayer. At Simply Smashed, we believe business isn't just about transactions. It's about strengthening the fabric of our community. It's about creating spaces where achievements like these are celebrated. Where young people feel seen, valued, and supported. Because when we uplift our youth, we elevate our entire community. When we celebrate their dedication, we inspire the next generation. When we show them we're proud, we give them the strength to continue. ↓ This Ramadan, let's commit to appreciating our Huffadh more. They're not just memorizing text - they're preserving our heritage, one verse at a time. Share this to show our young Huffadh: Your community stands with you. We see you. And we are incredibly proud.
